title: Paper 2 Question 3: language in non-fiction
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: Question 3 (AO2, 12 marks): language in a passage of one source

tips.title: A mark a minute
tips.body: Twelve marks, about twelve minutes. Three or four choices analysed in depth fill it; eight named do not. Then Question 4, which is worth sixteen.

tips.title: The focus is a condition
tips.body: The scheme says a student has to address the correct focus to reach Level 3 or above. Read the question's last words, night shifts, the encounter, the danger, and let them choose the details.

tips.title: Voice before images
tips.body: In non-fiction the first choice is who is speaking, to whom, and how. One sentence on the voice, tied to a quotation, sets up every image that follows.

tips.title: Name the job
tips.body: Non-fiction language has a purpose: to persuade, to move, to amuse, to make the reader see a real thing. Ending a point with what the writer wants the reader to feel about the real thing is the perceptive half of detailed and perceptive.

tips.title: Inside the lines, on the right source
tips.body: Outside the given lines or from the wrong source, the response goes to the bottom of its level. The passage was chosen so that the question can be answered from it.

tips.title: Understatement is a choice
tips.body: A calm voice about a dangerous thing is a method, not an absence of one. Shackleton's report on the worst sea in the world makes the reader supply the fear.

why.matters: Most of what a person reads in a life is non-fiction that wants something from them: an article that wants agreement, a speech that wants a vote, a memoir that wants sympathy, a report that wants trust. Every one of them is made of the choices Question 3 asks about, and the reader who can name the choice, the hyperbole that makes a joke of a horror, the exclamation that makes a writer present, the calm that makes danger credible, can see the work being done and decide whether to be moved by it. Twelve marks on the paper, and the rest of a reading life.

examples.title: The column and the campaign
examples.body: A newspaper column, a charity's appeal and a politician's speech use the June 2024 scheme's list, extended metaphor, juxtaposition, repetition, the triplet, direct address, to make a reader feel before they think. Naming the choice is the difference between being persuaded and deciding to be. The skill is the same one, and the diary passage was practice for the leaflet through the door.

examples.title: Writing that has to be trusted
examples.body: Shackleton's report on the worst sea in the world is the model for every account that has to be believed: a witness statement, a doctor's letter, an incident report, a leader explaining a hard decision. The calm is a choice, and the reader who can see it as one knows what the plain voice is doing, and can use it when their own account needs to be trusted.

steps.title: Question 3: twelve marks on one passage
steps.body:
Question 3 names one source and a passage of about ten lines, and asks how the writer uses language to do something. June 2024: Source A, lines 30 to 39; how does the writer use language to describe working night shifts at the hospital. Twelve marks, AO2, the same objective as Paper 1 Question 2 with half as many marks again.

**Four levels.** Level 4, 10 to 12: detailed, perceptive understanding of language, which the scheme spells out as analysing the effects of the writer's choices, selecting a range of judicious textual detail, and sophisticated and accurate use of terminology. Level 3, 7 to 9: clear, relevant explanation. Level 2, 4 to 6: some understanding and attempts to comment. Level 1, 1 to 3: simple, limited comment.

**Two rules in the scheme's notes.** A response about language outside the given lines, or from the wrong source, is placed at the bottom of whatever level its quality earns. And a student has to address the correct focus of the question to reach Level 3 or above: an answer about the passage that is not about night shifts stops at Level 2.

**Time.** About twelve minutes: a mark a minute.

rows: Detailed, perceptive: analyses effects; judicious detail; sophisticated terminology
Clear, relevant: explains effects clearly; relevant detail; clear terminology
Some understanding: attempts to comment on effect

steps.title: What the June 2024 scheme rewarded
steps.body:
The indicative content for the night-shift passage is a catalogue of the choices non-fiction writers make, each with the scheme's own quotation from the diary.

**An extended metaphor**, “sailing the ship alone”, developed into a ship that is “enormous, and on fire”: the Level 4 example read the ship as the writer's overwhelming responsibility, *alone* as the absence of support, and the fire as danger there is no escaping. **Juxtaposition**, in a hospital that “made Hell look like Disneyland”. **Adjectives**, “unrelenting” and “endless”. **Repetition**, “ward after ward, nurse after nurse, with emergency after emergency”. **A list, a triplet**, “one-man, mobile, essentially untrained A&E department”. **Metaphor**, an “unrelenting nightmare”. **Direct address**, “Your senior colleagues”. **Onomatopoeia**, the “bleep” of the pager.

Every one is a choice, and every one in the scheme's list is tied to the focus, the night shift. The Level 4 example took one, the extended metaphor, and went deep: scale against isolation, then fire as an inescapable fate.

columns: What it does to the night shift
rows: sailing the ship alone … enormous, and on fire
Comic exaggeration that measures the horror
ward after ward, nurse after nurse
The absurd scale of what one junior is
The reader put in the doctor's shoes

steps.title: Language in non-fiction: the same tools, different jobs
steps.body:
A diary, a memoir, a speech and an article use the techniques fiction uses, but they use them to persuade, to amuse, to move or to make a reader see a real place. Naming the job is part of the analysis.

**Seacole at the wharf.** The wounded artilleryman is “groaning heavily”; after she eases his dressings the groans subside into a “restless uneasy mutter”, and she breaks off: “God help him!” The exclamation is a prayer said aloud in the middle of a sentence, and it does what the description cannot: it lets the reader hear that she is moved. Then she raises tea to his “baked lips”, and the adjective, a word for bread and clay, makes the thirst physical.

**The job of each.** The sequence of sounds, groaning to muttering, lets the reader hear a man being eased; the prayer makes the writer present as a person, not a reporter; the one exact adjective makes the reader feel heat and thirst on their own mouth. Emotive language, exclamation and precise physical detail are the tools of a writer who wants the reader to care about a real man on a real wharf.

rows: The reader hears the man being eased
The writer present as a person who is moved
Thirst made physical, on the reader's own mouth
props.title: Seacole: four choices, four jobs

visuals.alt: A table of four language choices in the Seacole passage, each with its quotation and the job it does for a reader of non-fiction

check.prompt: What does the exclamation God help him! do in the middle of Seacole's description?
check.solution: The exclamation is a choice of sentence form and of voice: the writer steps out of describing and into feeling, for three words. Naming what it does for the reader, and for the writer's presence in her own account, is the analysis Question 3 rewards.

markScheme.description: It breaks the description with a prayer said aloud, so the reader hears that the writer is moved

It breaks the description with a prayer said aloud, so the reader hears that the writer is moved

steps.title: The practice passage: Shackleton makes the case
steps.body:
The second paragraph of the Shackleton passage, in which he argues the boat journey to his men. It is the passage for the questions that follow.

> The case required to be argued in some detail, since all hands knew that the perils of the proposed journey were extreme. The risk was justified solely by our urgent need of assistance. The ocean south of Cape Horn in the middle of May is known to be the most tempestuous storm-swept area of water in the world. The weather then is unsettled, the skies are dull and overcast, and the gales are almost unceasing. We had to face these conditions in a small and weather-beaten boat, already strained by the work of the months that had passed. Worsley and Wild realized that the attempt must be made, and they both asked to be allowed to accompany me on the voyage. I told Wild at once that he would have to stay behind. I relied upon him to hold the party together while I was away and to make the best of his way to Deception Island with the men in the spring in the event of our failure to bring help. Worsley I would take with me, for I had a very high opinion of his accuracy and quickness as a navigator, and especially in the snapping and working out of positions in difficult circumstances—an opinion that was only enhanced during the actual journey. Four other men would be required, and I decided to call for volunteers, although, as a matter of fact, I pretty well knew which of the people I would select. Crean I proposed to leave on the island as a right-hand man for Wild, but he begged so hard to be allowed to come in the boat that, after consultation with Wild, I promised to take him. I called the men together, explained my plan, and asked for volunteers. Many came forward at once. Some were not fit enough for the work that would have to be done, and others would not have been much use in the boat since they were not seasoned sailors, though the experiences of recent months entitled them to some consideration as seafaring men. McIlroy and Macklin were both anxious to go but realized that their duty lay on the island with the sick men. They suggested that I should take Blackborrow in order that he might have shelter and warmth as quickly as possible, but I had to veto this idea. It would be hard enough for fit men to live in the boat. Indeed, I did not see how a sick man, lying helpless in the bottom of the boat, could possibly survive in the heavy weather we were sure to encounter. I finally selected McNeish, McCarthy, and Vincent in addition to Worsley and Crean. The crew seemed a strong one, and as I looked at the men I felt confidence increasing.

**What to notice.** The superlative in “the most tempestuous storm-swept area of water in the world”; the plain triplet of the weather, unsettled, dull and overcast, gales almost unceasing; the boat that is “a small and weather-beaten boat, already strained”; and, against all of it, a tone that never raises its voice. The understatement is the choice: a writer who describes the worst sea in the world in the voice of a report makes the reader supply the fear he leaves out.

rows: the most tempestuous storm-swept area of water in the world
The scale of the danger stated once, absolutely
unsettled … dull and overcast … almost unceasing
Weather that does not let up, in a sentence that does not either
The means set against the danger
The case required to be argued in some detail
A report's voice for a decision about dying; the reader supplies the fear

steps.title: A Level 4 paragraph on Seacole
steps.body: The question: how does the writer use language to describe her first encounter with a wounded man? Here is one paragraph built to the descriptors.

visuals.problem: Write a Level 4 paragraph on the wounded artilleryman.

steps.text: Choose two details that build one impression: the man “groaning heavily” whose groans subside into a “restless uneasy mutter”.
steps.note: Judicious: a sequence, not two unconnected quotations.

steps.text: Name the choice: a sequence of sounds, from groan to mutter, carried by a verb of subsiding.
steps.note: Exact terminology: a sound sequence; the verb.

steps.text: Effect on the reader: the reader hears the man being eased before being told he has been, so the nursing is shown as a change in sound rather than claimed.
steps.note: Effect, and why the words produce it.

steps.text: Extend with a sentence form: the exclamation “God help him!” breaks the description, and the writer is suddenly present as a woman praying over a stranger.
steps.note: A second choice extends the first: sound, then voice.

steps.text: Finish on the physical: tea raised to his “baked lips”, an adjective from bread and clay that puts the man's thirst on the reader's own mouth, and makes the small act of a cup of tea the size it was to him.
steps.note: The last detail turns the paragraph back to the focus: the encounter.

steps.title: Tone and voice: the choices a non-fiction writer makes first
steps.body:
Before any image, a non-fiction writer chooses a voice, and the voice is made of language choices the examiners reward when they are named.

**Person and address.** Both June 2024 sources are first person; the doctor also uses direct address, *Your senior colleagues*, to put the reader in his place. Seacole addresses nobody and prays aloud instead.

**Tone.** The June 2024 scheme, for Question 4, called the doctor's tone humorous, sarcastic and caustic, and Seacole's emotive, serious and worthy. Each is built of choices: the diary's hyperbole, *made Hell look like Disneyland*; the memoir's exclamation and its poor fellow.

**Register.** Shackleton's report voice; a diary's casual *Sure …*; a memoir's formality. The register is a decision about how the reader is to be spoken to, and naming it is analysis.

**How to use it in Question 3.** One sentence on the voice, tied to a quotation, before the images: *The writer's caustic humour, in a hospital that made Hell look like Disneyland, sets the night shift up as something to be survived by joking.*

rows: First person, direct address, caustic humour
Exclamation; the poor fellow; God help him
Plain verbs; the case argued; superlative stated once

steps.title: Twelve marks: detailed, perceptive, on the focus
steps.body:
The Level 4 word for Paper 2 Question 3 is *detailed and perceptive*, and the twelve marks buy about three choices analysed in depth, not eight named.

**Three or four details, connected.** The Level 4 example took one metaphor and followed it through two quotations. Three such moves, each tied to the focus, fill twelve marks.

**The focus is the filter.** June 2024 asked about night shifts; every detail chosen had to describe the night shift, and the note in the scheme makes the focus a condition of Level 3. A brilliant paragraph on the writer's childhood would not pass it.

**Terminology sophisticated because exact.** Extended metaphor, juxtaposition, hyperbole, understatement, triplet, direct address, register: each names a choice the reader would otherwise miss. *Descriptive language* names nothing.

**Non-fiction has a job.** The best answers say what the writer wants the reader to think or feel about the real thing, and how the choice does it.

**Twelve minutes.** A mark a minute, then Question 4.

steps.title: Question 3 in one page
steps.body:
Twelve marks, twelve minutes, one passage of one source.

- **The shape:** how does the writer use language to …; the given lines only; the focus is a condition of Level 3.
- **Four levels:** detailed and perceptive at 10 to 12; clear and relevant at 7 to 9; some at 4 to 6; simple at 1 to 3.
- **The June 2024 list:** extended metaphor, juxtaposition, adjectives, repetition, triplet, metaphor, direct address, onomatopoeia; the Level 4 example went deep on one.
- **Non-fiction's tools have jobs:** to persuade, to move, to amuse, to make the reader see a real thing; name the job.
- **Voice first:** person, address, tone, register, each built from choices.
- **Three or four choices in depth,** connected, on the focus, with exact terms.

Practised on Seacole's wounded man and Shackleton's case for the voyage.

The exact term, then what it does to the reader
What the writer wants felt about the real thing

questions.prompt: How does the writer use language to describe her first encounter with a wounded man? Write a full Question 3 answer on the Seacole passage, from the artilleryman on the pallet to God bless you, of about the length you would write for twelve marks.
questions.solution: Seacole writes in the first person and in earnest, and the voice is set by the moment she stops describing and prays: “God help him!”, three words that break the sentence and let the reader hear a woman moved rather than a nurse reporting. The encounter is built first out of sound. The artilleryman is “groaning heavily”, and after she eases his dressings the groans subside into a “restless uneasy mutter”: the verb of subsiding and the two adjectives that qualify the mutter let the reader hear a man being eased before they are told he has been, so the nursing is shown as a change in sound rather than claimed. Then the writing turns physical. She raises tea to his “baked lips”, and the adjective, a word for bread and clay, makes the thirst something the reader feels on their own mouth, so that the small act of a metal cup of tea becomes the size it was to him. The final choice is the man's own voice, “God bless you, woman—whoever you are, God bless you!”, repeated, with the word woman doing the work: he cannot see her, and the discovery of a woman's hand on a wharf full of men is what the whole encounter has been leading to. Seacole wants the reader to feel that one wounded stranger was worth all of this, and every choice, the prayer, the sounds, the adjective, the repeated blessing, puts the reader beside the pallet to feel it.

questions.prompt: How does the writer use language to convey the danger of the boat journey? Write a full Question 3 answer on the second paragraph of the Shackleton passage, of about the length you would write for twelve marks.
questions.solution: Shackleton conveys the danger by refusing to raise his voice about it. The register is a report's: the case, he says, “required to be argued in some detail”, and the phrase treats a decision about dying as an item of business, so that the reader hears the calm and supplies the fear it leaves out. Into that calm he places one absolute, “the most tempestuous storm-swept area of water in the world”, a superlative stated once and left, without image or exclamation, which makes it heavier than any image would be. The weather is then listed in plain adjectives, unsettled, dull and overcast, the gales almost unceasing, and the list itself does not let up, so the reader feels the conditions as something continuous rather than dramatic. Against the ocean he sets the means: “a small and weather-beaten boat, already strained”, and the three adjectives, each smaller than the last, let the reader do the arithmetic between the sea and the boat before the voyage has begun. The understatement is the method. A writer who wanted only to frighten would have exclaimed; Shackleton wants the reader to understand a decision, and the plainness of the language is what makes the danger, and the courage of the men who asked to go, credible.

questions.prompt: A student writes: 'Seacole uses emotive language to make the reader feel sorry for the man.' Why is this Level 2 rather than Level 4?
questions.solution: Emotive language is a label for a whole class of choices. The mark is for the choice itself, the poor fellow or God help him, and for how those words make the reader feel what they feel. A category with a feeling attached is an attempt to comment, the Level 2 wording.

questions.prompt: A student says: 'Non-fiction is just facts, so there is less language to analyse than in fiction.' What is the better account?
questions.solution: A diary, a memoir and a report are made of choices as much as a story is, and their choices have a job: to persuade, to move, to make a reader see. The scheme found an extended metaphor, juxtaposition, repetition, a triplet, direct address and onomatopoeia in ten lines of a diary.

examTechnique.body:
**One source, one passage, one focus.** Twelve marks, AO2, about twelve minutes. Outside the lines or the wrong source goes to the bottom of the level; off the focus cannot reach Level 3.

**Voice first.** Person, address, tone, register, in one sentence tied to a quotation.

**Three or four choices in depth.** Connected, on the focus, each named exactly and analysed for effect and reason. The June 2024 Level 4 example went deep on one extended metaphor.

**Name the job.** What the writer wants the reader to feel about the real thing. Non-fiction's tools persuade, move, amuse and make the reader see.

**Terminology that names a choice:** extended metaphor, juxtaposition, hyperbole, understatement, triplet, direct address, register. Not descriptive language.
examinerErrors: Listing eight techniques with a line each, which is identification, not analysis.
Analysing language outside the given lines, or from the wrong source.
Losing the focus: writing about the passage rather than about the thing the question names.
Naming a tone or a category, emotive language, without the choice that makes it or its effect.
Treating a plain, understated passage as having nothing to analyse.
Spending twenty minutes on twelve marks and leaving Question 4 short.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer opens with the voice, named as a choice and tied to a quotation, and then takes three or four details that build one impression of the thing the question names, each with its exact term, its effect on the reader and the reason the words produce it. It reads tone as made of choices, treats understatement as a method, and ends each point on what the writer wants the reader to feel about a real place or person. It stays inside the lines and on the focus, and it takes about twelve minutes.
